Cube Land: How Rotatelab Built a Hit From Gaziantep

Cube Land: How Rotatelab Built a Hit From Gaziantep
Nov 9
Written by
Aylin Yazıcı
Written by
Aylin
, your former Puzzle Addict.
Cube Land has been one of the most talked-about puzzle launches of the summer. It went live globally on July 2, and within weeks, it was in the US top 50 free and top 80 grossing charts. The studio behind it, Rotatelab, is based in Gaziantep, a city in southeastern Türkiye, more than a thousand kilometers from Istanbul, where most of the country's game industry sits.
View fullsize
How Rotatelab got here is the bigger story. The team spent years shipping games, left the publisher model when they felt ready, spent a year and a half learning to self-publish with Sort Land, and put the whole studio behind Cube Land once its retention test came back. They did all of it from Gaziantep with a team spread across the country. Cube Land is what that path produced, and I think the path deserves as much attention as the game.
Ten years of shipping
The founders have been making games together since 2016. They founded Rotatelab in 2020 and spent about 2.5 years working with Rollic on hyper-casual titles. Over that period, their games passed 17 million lifetime installs, and one of them reached #1 on the US App Store free chart.
They have launched around 20 games over the years, and that number leaves out every prototype that died in testing. I read that number as a record of how many times this team went through the full cycle of building, testing, and killing a game. I see hit-making in this genre as a numbers game, and the studios that get there are usually the ones that kept taking shots long after most teams would have given up.
In August, Rotatelab closed a seed round co-led by Laton Ventures and Arcadia Gaming Partners.
November to March
The idea for Cube Land came up in November 2025, and development started at the end of December. The first marketability test ran in January 2026, around the time the market was moving toward pixel-style art because it brought cheaper installs. Results were good enough for two months of focused production. The retention test at the end of March held up, and after that, the whole studio moved onto the game.
About 4 months passed between the idea and a validated game. Rotatelab says it built its own AI tools covering market analysis, playable prototypes, and marketing automation, and this timeline supports that claim better than any press release could. I'll be more convinced when those tools start producing levels at the pace the game needs, which I come back to at the end.
Rotation changes the level design
View fullsize
Cube Land comes from the This is Blast family, and I'd place it closer to This is Blast than to Pixel Flow. There's a queue of color shooters, a small bench, and a block picture you clear by firing shooters in the right order. Pixel Flow added a conveyor belt for the cannons, while Cube Land has none. It turns the picture into a 3D voxel object that the player rotates and adds the layered structure we saw in Screwdom and Yarn Loop, where each model is cleared from the outside in.
Screwdom made a similar move when it took Screw Jam's flat board and turned it into 3D objects. With an object, a level designer can hide cubes behind other cubes, spread one color across several sides, and build inner layers that only open once the outer shell is gone. The player makes two decisions per move: which shooter to fire and which side of the object to face.
Most sort games released this year only asked for the first one. Turning the object to line up a shot also feels much better in the hand than tapping at a flat grid, and I'd put Cube Land next to Screwdom as one of the cleanest iterations this genre has seen.
The blockers are standard for the genre, including hidden and linked shooters. The layering does most of the new work, and I expect later levels to lean on it much more than on new blocker types. Sort puzzlers have never needed long mechanic curves. A big part of the pleasure is the object itself and peeling it apart layer by layer, so I think the choice of what goes on the block matters almost as much as the mechanics do.
The fail condition is the design detail I like best. Most games in this family end the level when the bench fills up. Cube Land ends it when the bench is full, and none of your shooters can reach a visible cube of their color. Before that point, the game rotates the object by itself to search for a valid shot. Players who rotate with intent still clear levels more efficiently than the auto-spin, but nobody loses because they missed a single blue cube on the far side of the model.
View fullsize
The difficulty sits in the queue
Rotating the object is the part of Cube Land that feels most like skill. When you look at how levels are actually lost, rotation is rarely the reason. Levels are usually lost to the shooters you can't see yet, deeper in the queue. An early pick from the wrong column leaves the colors you need buried, and a few moves later, the bench is full.
This setup suits a hybrid game well. Players act freely in the parts they enjoy, and the designers tune the difficulty in the parts players can't fully read. When a booster or an extra bench slot shows up at that moment, it feels like help, which makes it easier to buy.
It’s easier to get through the first hundred levels without much resistance. I think the easy stretch is intentional. Puzzle players who are going to pay tend to do it within their first couple of hours, so it makes sense to keep them moving through levels during that window and let interstitials take over after it.
With an ad after nearly every level in that stretch, the early game carries a lot of the ad monetization. There is a cooldown, so quick consecutive fails don't each trigger an ad, and ads start at different points in their progress, which suggests segmentation by UA source or country.
